source.title: Neurograf v1: An End-to-End Romanian-First Language Model Family

record.tranche_reason: It measures validation loss across a controlled family of new language models and estimates a compute-optimal scaling relation, using scaling analyses comparable to those in the original sources.
record.gate_note: The study reports fixed-data validation-loss fits, compute-optimal parameter estimates, SFT loss comparisons, and downstream benchmark evaluations. The fixed-data fit's extrapolated target losses are estimates, not validation against larger trained runs; these do not establish extrapolation accuracy. Other corpus, tokenizer, and embedding results do not bear on the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study trains its own five-model family (160M–6B) on one fixed 131B-token Romanian stream. It fits validation bits-per-byte against parameter count with a Chinchilla/Kaplan-form law (E + A·N^-α) and estimates compute-optimal parameter count from iso-FLOP slices with a quadratic-vertex method, fitting Nopt ∝ C^0.423. It also relates downstream WWTBM accuracy to log parameter count. These are the original sources' methods and measures applied in a new language setting. The only departure is that the iso-FLOP points come from intermediate checkpoints of warmup–stable–decay runs rather than separate runs.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that validation BPB improves with model size at fixed data along a power law with a floor and strongly diminishing returns. They find the compute-optimal parameter exponent is about 0.423, shallower than Chinchilla's 0.50, so token exposure is relatively more valuable. They treat this as specific to this corpus, model family and checkpoint-based construction, noting possible curvature and schedule bias. To add: they also conclude that factual WWTBM knowledge scales strongly and roughly log-linearly with capacity, heterogeneously across topics, while simple grammar saturates early. For SFT they find only a monotonic, diminishing advantage of scale and decline to fit a law.
record.recipe_differences: Scaling measurements use a fixed-data five-model family for validation BPB and derive compute-optimal points from intermediate checkpoints using quadratic interpolation in log parameter count. The paper also reports limited SFT and downstream scaling comparisons.
record.method_sensitivity: The compute-optimal estimate depends on checkpoint interpolation and sampling during the warmup–stable–decay schedule; many intermediate checkpoints lack terminal decay. The authors also report possible high-compute curvature. The external WWTBM comparison changes continuation-length normalization from tokens to UTF-8 bytes because tokenizers differ.
record.problems: Only five base-model sizes and one training run per size are used; the fixed-data fit has only two residual degrees of freedom. The compute-optimal points come from intermediate checkpoints rather than independent runs, and schedule bias is unquantified. The compute range is below the full training compute of the two largest models, and the authors report systematic high-compute deviations. SFT comparisons cover only three sizes and stopped while loss was still decreasing. WWTBM confidence intervals measure question-sample uncertainty, not training-seed variation.
record.rows_left_out: The five final grammar-probe margins in Section 5.2 and checkpoint-by-checkpoint WWTBM trajectories in Sections 5.3 and 5.6 were not extracted because the 60-row limit was reached; the final WWTBM scale outcomes and topic-specific results were prioritized. The fixed-data target-loss extrapolations in Table 11 are not measurements on larger trained runs and were therefore not recorded as tested outcomes.

untested.parts: Loss scaling in tokens or compute with parameters non-limiting (data is fixed here). Coverage of several orders of magnitude: the sizes span only about 36×.
All of it. The Table 11 parameter counts implied by target losses are extrapolations never checked against trained larger runs.
A separately fitted exponent for loss-minimising token count. Behaviour above 1.1E21 FLOP, which is below the full compute of the two largest runs. Independent fully scheduled runs at each budget.
All of it. Depth and width are scaled together at a fixed aspect ratio of 128, never varied at fixed parameter count.
All of it. The SFT comparison has three sizes with no fitted law. Other modalities, repeated-data laws and transfer are not studied.
Prediction from pretraining loss rather than parameter count. Tasks beyond WWTBM and the grammar probe. Behaviour outside 160M–6B.

missing.what: The fixed-data loss-law fit itself: E=0.4366, A=0.2602, α=0.3047, R²=0.999993, RMSE 2.86E-4 BPB, maximum residual 5.25E-4, two residual degrees of freedom.
Overall WWTBM accuracy fitted against log10 N: 19.55 pp per parameter decade, R²=0.975, 29.1 pp gain from 160M to 6B.

record.verdict_notes: Labelled T1 because the methods match the originals (Chinchilla-form loss fit, iso-FLOP quadratic vertex), though in a new language setting; T3 would also be defensible. The study is not an original source. The SFT rows (R36–R39) are approximate training-loss gaps read from a plot, with three sizes and no law, so V5 gets no verdict. External comparator rows (R49–R54) are unlinked. R35 duplicates topics already covered by R23–R34.

versions.untested_parts: Token-count and compute scaling of held-out pretraining loss with the other quantities non-bottlenecking; several-orders-of-magnitude coverage.
No larger runs are trained to check whether predictions fitted on smaller runs are accurate.
A direct fitted power law for the loss-minimising token count versus compute; behavior outside the measured compute range.
Depth, width, and other architecture details are not independently varied at a fixed parameter count.
Other modalities, repeated-data regimes, transfer, and fine-tuning power laws beyond the limited SFT scale comparison.
Downstream tasks beyond the reported Romanian grammar probe and WWTBM benchmark; prediction beyond the measured model range.
The effects of varying parameter-count conventions, fitting methods, data, and schedules are not systematically isolated.

rows.subject: Neurograf base-model family
rows.operation_detail: Interpolated twenty iso-FLOP slices and fitted compute-optimal parameter count against compute.
rows.measure: Exponent for Nopt versus compute; R²
rows.note: A power-law parameter trend is reported, but it is shallower than the reference and does not directly fit optimal token count.
rows.check: For V3, a stable power law in compute is observed (R²=0.988 over about 1E19–1.1E21 FLOP). The exponent 0.423 implies tokens grow faster than parameters, matching neither Kaplan's nor Hoffmann's split. For V7 the row is also observed, since the exponent departs from the 0.50 reference. Marking it 'partial' conflated the exponent's value with whether the power-law form holds. Points are interpolated from intermediate warmup–stable–decay checkpoints, so schedule bias is unquantified.

rows.value: The highest compute optima fall systematically below the fitted power-law line.
rows.note: The authors say this may indicate a changing effective exponent or checkpoint-schedule bias; they cannot distinguish the explanations.
rows.check: Partial for V3: the power law bends at the highest budgets. Observed for V7: the curve departs from a single power law. The authors cannot separate real curvature from checkpoint-schedule bias.

source_check.correct: State: partial for V3; observed for V7. The reported high-compute curvature qualifies a stable allocation power and directly exhibits departure from a single power law.
